comparison: Both strongly support the core finding that age-dependent plasticity enables rapid learning and slow forgetting (C1, C2, C16-C19, C65-C66). OpenEval emphasizes Figure 2C computational evidence; peer reviewers affirm this as the central mechanism with editor and Reviewer 1 highlighting transient properties of adult-born neurons. Peer review also includes C3, C68-C70 (enhanced excitability) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

OpenEval R2 addresses enhanced excitability (C3, C20, C67-C70, C75-C76, C80-C81) as a distinct mechanism supported by Figures 2E, 2G, 2I-J. Peer R1 includes some overlapping claims (C3, C68-C70) within the broader flexibility-stability resolution. Both support these findings, though OpenEval provides more granular analysis of excitability's specific role.

Both address enhanced excitability and apoptosis mechanisms. OpenEval R2 focuses on excitability preventing learning deficits (C20, C75-C76); peer R2 emphasizes apoptosis maintaining flexibility (C20-C21, C72-C76). Limited overlap (C20, C75-C76) but complementary focus on different aspects of the maturation process.

Both support apoptosis-related findings. OpenEval R3 addresses growth saturation, selective apoptosis, and flexibility maintenance (C21, C48-C54, C99-C100, C102-C103, C108, C114, C173) with Figures 4B-E, 5C. Peer R5 accepts apoptosis predictions (C27, C99-C103, C108-C109, C114, C173, C175) noting importance for continual learning. Strong agreement on apoptosis function.

Both address experimental grounding of apoptosis implementation. OpenEval R3 includes claims about apoptosis patterns matching experiments (C48-C54); peer R9 accepts the apoptosis mechanism as biologically grounded (C47-C54). Overlap on C48-C51 with agreement on biological plausibility.

Both support preferential recruitment of young neurons. OpenEval R4 emphasizes two GC clusters, odor-specific connectivity, and sensory-dependent dendritic elaboration (C22-C23, C77-C90) with Figures 2H-I, 3C. Peer R3 affirms the model captures experimental observations about preferential recruitment and memory extinction (C22-C23, C79-C81, C84-C86, C89-C90). Strong agreement on this mechanism.

Both strongly support the re-learning prediction. OpenEval R5 details re-recruitment of original neurons and faster re-learning (C25-C26, C91-C98, C122, C164-C166) with Figure 3E-F as testable prediction. Peer R4 treats these predictions positively (C25-C26, C91-C98, C164-C166), with Reviewer 3 specifically noting the combination leads to experimentally testable hypotheses. Near-perfect agreement (Jaccard 0.929).

Both support findings about stable memory traces and systematic ablation results. OpenEval R6 emphasizes Figure 5B-G showing graded retention and dissecting contributions of apoptosis, excitability, and neurogenesis (C27, C104-C115, C121). Peer R6 affirms these as key results (C104-C107, C111-C113, C115, C121-C122) providing coherent picture. Strong agreement (Jaccard 0.643).

Both support baseline comparison showing age-dependent properties are essential. OpenEval R7 addresses C62-C63 with Figure 2C showing no difference between neurogenic and non-neurogenic models with uniform synapses. Peer R10 includes C62-C63 within broader acceptance of model features (C55-C63, C67). Agreement on this critical control.

Both support memory capacity scaling analysis. OpenEval R8 addresses theoretical analysis (C124-C125) showing √N scaling in Appendix 2. Peer R12 includes C124-C125 within broader acceptance of functional arguments and evolutionary rationale (C71, C124-C147, C153). Agreement on computational efficiency claims.

Both support integration of experimental observations with model interpretations. OpenEval R9 addresses retrograde interference and rapid re-learning interpretation (C143-C147) with Figure 4—figure supplement 2. Peer R12 includes C143-C147 within acceptance of broader interpretations and functional arguments. Agreement on these integrative claims.

Both strongly support model architecture and implementation. OpenEval R10 details architecture based on OB anatomy and calcium-based plasticity (C30-C46) with Figure 1A-C. Peer R8 accepts model architecture and approach (C28-C46), with Reviewer 3 confirming systematic model building and biological plausibility. Very strong agreement (Jaccard 0.842).

Both support age-dependent spine turnover calibration. OpenEval R11 addresses C59, C64 with Figure 2A and quantitative fit to Sailor et al. 2016. Peer R7 includes C64 within broader affirmation of model capturing experimental data (C4, C24, C64). Agreement on experimental grounding.

Both support basic learning/forgetting dynamics. OpenEval R12 addresses C60-C61 with Figure 2B showing MC activity patterns. Peer R10 includes C60-C61 within acceptance of model features and results (C55-C63, C67). Agreement on capturing basic dynamics.

Both support the computational problem that excitability solves. OpenEval R13 addresses accumulation preventing learning (C71-C74) with Figure 2G and citations. Peer R2 includes C72-C74 within acceptance of excitability and apoptosis mechanisms (C20-C21, C72-C76). Agreement on this foundational issue.

Both support cross-regional validation. OpenEval R14 addresses C83 with citation to Adlaf et al. 2017 and Figure 2H connectivity analysis. Peer R11 includes C83 within acceptance of network organization findings (C77-C78, C82-C83, C87-C88). Agreement on hippocampal comparison.

Both support selective apoptosis patterns. OpenEval R15 addresses C101 with Figure 4C and citation to Mouret et al. 2008. Peer R5 includes C101 within acceptance of apoptosis findings (C27, C99-C103, C108-C109, C114, C173, C175). Agreement on experimental validation.

Both support permanent encoding control simulation. OpenEval R16 addresses C116-C120 with Figure 5G-H showing this variant dissects spontaneous plasticity versus overwriting. Peer R6 implicitly includes this within systematic ablation results (C104-C107, C111-C113, C115, C121-C122). Agreement on control analysis.

Both support robustness to doubled neurogenesis. OpenEval R17 addresses C178 with Figure 4—figure supplement 1. Peer R14 includes C178 within acceptance of predictions and experimental connections (C167-C172, C174, C176-C183). Agreement on robustness check.

Peer R8 includes C28-C29 within acceptance of model architecture (C28-C46), with Reviewer 1 noting experimental basis provides excellent foundation. Agreement on contextual grounding.

Both support general model-experiment correspondence. OpenEval R19 addresses C4, C58 as summary claims about model validation. Peer R7 includes C4 within consistent affirmation that model captures diverse experimental data (C4, C24, C64). Agreement on overall validation.

Both support high-level conclusions about flexibility-stability resolution. OpenEval R20 addresses C5-C6, C141, C153 as main interpretive conclusions from Figures 2-5. Peer R1 includes C5-C6 within affirmation of core finding (C1-C3, C5-C6, C16-C19, C65-C66, C68-C70). Agreement on central conclusions.

Both support evolutionary and functional rationale. OpenEval R21 addresses C126-C140 about why OB uses neurogenesis with citations and logical reasoning. Peer R12 includes C126-C140 within acceptance of broader interpretations (C71, C124-C147, C153). Strong agreement on functional arguments (Jaccard 0.577).

Peer R12 includes C142 within acceptance of functional arguments (C71, C124-C147, C153). Agreement that this is reasonable speculation.

OpenEval R26 addresses C55-C57 about sensory refinement versus reinforcement. Peer R10 includes C55-C57 within acceptance of model features (C55-C63, C67). Agreement on functional interpretation of neurogenesis role.

Peer R15 includes C191-C206 within acceptance of limitations and future directions. Strong agreement on scope discussion (Jaccard 0.571).

OpenEval R13 addresses computational problem of accumulation (C71-C74). Peer R12 includes C71 within broader acceptance of functional arguments (C71, C124-C147, C153). Agreement on this foundational computational issue.
